newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain hopes austere budget will secure EMU goal. [CORRECTED 12:12 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Spain hopes austere budget will secure EMU goal. [CORRECTED 12:12 GMT]

text.p: Spanish Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato on Monday delivered to parliament an austere budget which the conservative government hopes will place Spain among the first group of countries to join a European single currency.
The 54-volume draft, whose broad contents were unveiled on Friday, is certain to be passed despite drawing sharp criticism from the leftist opposition at the weekend.
The minority Popular Party (PP) has already secured the backing of its Catalan nationalist allies in parliament, ensuring the budget will be voted through.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar reaffirmed his country's commitment to being among the first wave of single currency nations, a key platform of his campaign in the general election he won in March.

"We will be there," Aznar told the Financial Times in an interview published on Monday. "I am ready to take whatever measures are necessary to succeed, because I am absolutely persuaded that Spain is staking its stability and prosperity in this bet."
The 1997 budget package slashes total spending growth to just 1.7
(Corrects from "slashes total spending to ...).
percent by cutting or freezing spending in all sectors except for pensions, health and regional transfers.
With inflation expected to grow 2.6 percent next year, this makes it the most restrictive budget since Spain's return to democracy in 1975.
The budget deficit is forecast to drop to three percent of gross domestic product next year, the level required to join a European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Nevertheless, the government forecasts a healthy 3.0 percent growth in 1997 and foresees the creation of 200,000 jobs.

"The budget will put the Spanish economy on the European horizon in the way Spaniards desire - with reasonable efforts directed especially to the public sector," Rato said at a press conference following the official presentation.

Market reaction was sanguine, with analysts saying Monday's detailed budget figures offered few surprises and paved the way for the Bank of Spain to cut its key money market rate -- the rate at which it lends to banks -- from 7.25 percent.
Traders have already discounted a cut of between 25 and 50 basis points at the central bank's regular auction on Thursday.

"By helping achieve economic stability, this budget raises the degree of confidence in the Spanish economy from the point of view of its citizens as well as from the persective of international markets," Rato said.
But unions and left-wing parties attacked the plan, saying that despite its lofty goals it lacks credibility and places the burden of budget adjustment on the poorest sectors of society.
Unions on Monday launched the first in a series of protests against a public sector wage freeze, claiming it will cut 1997 forecast growth by 0.7 percent and create 100,000 fewer jobs.

"We hope that from now until December, this government changes its attitude, because if it doesn't the unions will consider stronger pressure methods," said Enrique Alonso of the Confederation of Independent and Public Sector Unions.
Syndicates are planning a second protest on October 15 which could herald a prolonged period of confrontation between workers and the government, which insists the decision is irreversible.

Meanwhile the Socialists, in opposition after 13 years at the helm, backed the PP's commitment to EMU but criticised the means. They accused the conservatives of short-termism, saying their figures were over-optimistic and didn't add up.
Rato on Monday rejected accusations his government was viewing the future through rose-tinted glasses. "We consider that our forecasts for revenue and expenditure are absolutely reasonable," he said.
Although the opposition has the power to send the draft back for amendments, the government is ultimately safe in the knowledge its powerful Catalan allies will help push it through.
Jordi Pujol, leader of the Catalan Convergence and Unity (CiU) coalition, has declared himself broadly satisfied with the plan and said the Bank of Spain should now cut official rates.
